title: Scammers Have Moved from Email to Phone: Microsoft Gives Teams an AI Anti-Fraud Agent

content_html:
The main battleground for phishing attacks is quietly expanding from email inboxes to phone lines—a panicked-sounding "IT support call" is often harder to see through than a suspicious email. On November 24, according to a report yesterday by tech media outlet Neowin, Microsoft is developing an AI anti-scam feature for Teams that analyzes conversation content during calls and warns users once it detects signs of a potential phishing scam. According to Microsoft's roadmap, the feature is planned to be available to all users in January 2027.

Focusing on scripts that impersonate IT administrators

The feature applies to one-on-one external calls, and its target is signs of voice phishing scams. A typical scenario: scammers impersonate IT administrators and call employees, using excuses such as "account anomaly" and "system upgrade" to create urgency and trick them into handing over login credentials—these scripts are the key detection target of the new feature. Once matched, the system pops up a warning window to remind the person on the call to be careful.

From "blocking calls" to "listening to content"

Teams previously had some suspicious-call protection, such as nuisance call identification and spam call detection, but those defenses stopped at "before answering." The new feature extends screening to the call content itself: even if a user accidentally answers a scam call, the system can assess it while the conversation is ongoing, promptly prompt them to cut losses before damage occurs, and move the remediation window from "reporting after the fact" to "during the call."

There is still an unresolved detail: Microsoft has not said whether the related analysis is performed locally on the device or uploaded to the cloud for processing. Before AI monitoring of call content becomes the norm, this question will likely be hard to avoid.
